A **real Hilbert space** is a real inner-product space $H$ ([[def-real-and-complex-inner-product-space]]) whose induced-length metric is complete in the sense of [[def-complete-metric-space]]: every Cauchy sequence in $H$ for the norm $\|v\|=\sqrt{\langle v,v\rangle}$ ([[cor-inner-product-induces-a-norm]]) converges to a point of $H$. A **complex Hilbert space** is a complex inner-product space with the same completeness property, so that a Hilbert space is exactly a real or complex inner-product space that is a Banach space for its induced norm ([[def-banach-space]]).

**The completion convention is the Cauchy-sequence one.**
[[def-banach-space]] defines completeness by convergence of Cauchy sequences, and this page keeps that convention throughout. It is weaker than $\sigma$-completeness — the assertion that every decreasing sequence of nonempty closed subsets with diameters tending to zero has a nonempty intersection. The two agree in ZFC, but Blackadar, Farah and Karagila note that the closest-point theorem on a $\sigma$-complete inner-product space is provable in ZF, whereas the Cauchy-complete form used below consumes the Axiom of Countable Choice; nothing here silently imports the stronger notion.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $T$ be a
densely defined linear operator on $H$, with domain $D(T)$ dense in $H$
([[def-densely-defined-closed-and-closable-operator]], [[def-dense-top]]).
Since $D(T)$ is dense, and since $H$ is complete ([[def-hilbert-space]]), every
bounded linear functional on the normed space $(D(T),\|\cdot\|)$
([[def-bounded-linear-operator]]) extends uniquely to a bounded linear
functional $\widetilde\varphi$ on $H$ of the same norm, by setting
$\widetilde\varphi(z)=\lim_n\varphi(z_n)$ for any sequence $z_n\in D(T)$ with
$z_n\to z$ in $H$; the limit exists because $\varphi$ is bounded on a dense
subspace and $H$ is complete, and it does not depend on the sequence because a
bounded functional is uniformly continuous.

A vector $y\in H$ belongs to the **adjoint domain** $D(T^*)$ when the linear
functional $\varphi_y:D(T)\to\mathbb C$, $\varphi_y(x)=\langle Tx,y\rangle$, is
bounded on $(D(T),\|\cdot\|)$. In that case Hilbert space Riesz representation
([[thm-riesz-representation-for-hilbert-space]]) applied to the extension
$\widetilde{\varphi_y}$ produces a unique vector $T^*y\in H$ with
$$T^*y\text{ is the unique }w\in H\text{ such that }\langle Tx,y\rangle=\langle x,w\rangle\quad\text{for all }x\in D(T),$$
equivalently $\widetilde{\varphi_y}(z)=\langle z,T^*y\rangle$ for all $z\in H$.
The map $T^*:D(T^*)\to H$, $y\mapsto T^*y$, is the **adjoint** of $T$.

**Well-definedness.** The functional $\varphi_y$ is linear in $x$ for each
$y$, so its domain of boundedness $D(T^*)$ is a linear subspace: if
$\varphi_y,\varphi_{y'}$ are bounded so is $\varphi_{ay+by'}$ for scalars
$a,b$, because the first-variable-linear convention gives
$\varphi_{ay+by'}=\overline a\,\varphi_y+\overline b\,\varphi_{y'}$. On
$D(T^*)$ the map $T^*$ is linear: if $y,y'$ are represented by $w,w'$, then
$ay+by'$ is represented by $aw+bw'$, since
$\langle x,aw+bw'\rangle=\overline a\langle x,w\rangle+
\overline b\langle x,w'\rangle$; the representing vector is unique. By Riesz representation for the Hilbert space
$H$ a vector $w\in H$ is determined by the values $\langle z,w\rangle$ with
$z$ ranging over $H$, and those values are determined by the functional
$\widetilde{\varphi_y}$. Equivalently, if $w,w'$ both represent $\varphi_y$,
then $\langle x,w-w'\rangle=0$ for every $x\in D(T)$; density of $D(T)$ and
continuity of the inner product extend this equality to every $x\in H$, and
taking $x=w-w'$ gives $w=w'$. Finally only
ambient-norm boundedness of $\varphi_y$ on $D(T)$ is required: no extension,
no closure and no closedness of $T$ is presupposed.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $T$ be a densely defined linear operator on $H$.

- $T$ is **symmetric** when $T\subseteq T^*$, that is, $D(T)\subseteq D(T^*)$ and
  $Tx=T^*x$ for all $x\in D(T)$; equivalently
  $\langle Tx,y\rangle=\langle x,Ty\rangle$ for all $x,y\in D(T)$.
- $T$ is **self-adjoint** when $T=T^*$, that is, the domains and the values
  agree.
- $T$ is **essentially self-adjoint** when its closure $\overline T$ is
  self-adjoint; by [[thm-closable-iff-adjoint-domain-is-dense]] this presupposes
  that $T$ is closable.

**Consequences, with proofs.** These are part of the content of the definition.

1. *A symmetric $T$ is closable.* $T\subseteq T^*$ and $T^*$ is closed
   ([[lem-unbounded-adjoint-is-well-defined-and-closed]]), so $T^*$ is a closed
   extension of $T$. In particular the closure $\overline T$ exists and
   $\overline T\subseteq T^*$.
2. *The closure of a symmetric operator is symmetric.* If $T\subseteq T^*$,
   the inclusion reversal of
   [[lem-unbounded-adjoint-is-well-defined-and-closed]] applied to
   $T\subseteq T^*$ gives $(T^*)^*\subseteq T^*$, that is
   $T^{**}\subseteq T^*$. Applying it once more to the inclusion
   $T^{**}\subseteq T^*$ gives $(T^*)^*\subseteq(T^{**})^*$, that is
   $T^{**}\subseteq T^{***}$. Since $\overline T=T^{**}$ and
   $(\overline T)^*=T^{***}$
   ([[thm-closable-iff-adjoint-domain-is-dense]]), this reads
   $\overline T\subseteq(\overline T)^*$: the closure is symmetric. (Each
   application is legitimate because the adjoint is defined once its operator
   is densely defined, and $D(T^{**})$ is dense because
   $T\subseteq T^{**}=\overline T$, so that $D(T^{**})$ contains the dense
   domain $D(T)$.)
3. *A self-adjoint operator has no proper symmetric extension.* If $T=T^*$ and
   $T\subseteq S\subseteq S^*$, then $S^*\subseteq T^*$ by inclusion reversal,
   so $T\subseteq S\subseteq S^*\subseteq T^*=T$ and all inclusions are
   equalities.
4. *A self-adjoint operator is closed*, being equal to the adjoint $T^*$ of the
   densely defined $T$, and *an essentially self-adjoint operator has exactly
   one self-adjoint extension*, namely $\overline T$: a self-adjoint extension
   $S$ of $T$ is closed, hence contains the least closed extension
   $\overline T$, and then $S\subseteq S^*\subseteq(\overline T)^*=\overline T$
   by item 2 and symmetry, so $S=\overline T$.

Let $X$ and $Y$ be normed spaces over the same scalar field $\mathbb K$, read in
the real case from [[def-norm-and-normed-space]] and in the complex case from
[[rem-real-and-complex-normed-space-convention]]. A linear map
$T:X\to Y$ ([[def-linear-map]]) is a **bounded linear operator** when there is a
real constant $C \ge 0$ such that

$$\|Tx\| \le C\|x\| \qquad \text{for all } x \in X.$$

Any such $C$ is called a **bound** for $T$.

Let $X$ and $Y$ be normed spaces over the same scalar field, and let
$T:X\to Y$ be bounded in the sense of [[def-bounded-linear-operator]]. The
**operator norm** of $T$ is

$$\|T\| := \sup\{\|Tx\| : x \in X,\ \|x\| \le 1\}.$$

The set on the right contains $0$ and every bound $C$ for $T$ bounds it
above. Thus its finite real supremum exists by the proved least-upper-bound
property of the library's real field ([[cor-cauchy-reals-lub-complete]]).
In particular every number strictly below the supremum is exceeded by a
member of this set; otherwise it would be a smaller upper bound. No choice
principle is used for this assertion.

The same number is the least bound of $T$:

$$\|T\| = \inf\{C \ge 0 : \|Tx\| \le C\|x\| \text{ for all } x \in X\}.$$

If $X \ne \{0\}$, positive homogeneity also gives

$$\|T\| = \sup\{\|Tx\| : \|x\| = 1\}.$$

When $X = \{0\}$, the unit sphere is empty and the unit-ball supremum is $0$,
so $\|T\| = 0$.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $H$ and $K$ be real or complex Hilbert spaces and let $T\in\mathcal B(H,K)$ be a bounded linear operator ([[def-bounded-linear-operator]], [[def-space-of-bounded-linear-operators]]). For fixed $y\in K$ the map

$$x\longmapsto\langle Tx,y\rangle_K$$

is a bounded linear functional on $H$: it is linear in $x$ because $T$ is linear and the pairing is linear in its first argument, and $|\langle Tx,y\rangle_K|\le\|Tx\|\,\|y\|\le\|T\|\,\|x\|\,\|y\|$ by Cauchy–Schwarz and the operator-norm inequality ([[thm-cauchy-schwarz-in-an-inner-product-space]], [[def-operator-norm]]). By Riesz representation ([[thm-riesz-representation-for-hilbert-space]]) there is therefore a unique vector $T^*y\in H$ with

$$\langle Tx,y\rangle_K=\langle x,T^*y\rangle_H\qquad\text{for every }x\in H .$$

The **Hilbert adjoint** of $T$ is the map

$$T^*:K\longrightarrow H,\qquad y\longmapsto T^*y .$$

It is the unique map $K\to H$ satisfying the displayed identity, since two such maps have $\langle x,(T^*_1-T^*_2)y\rangle=0$ for all $x$ and hence $(T^*_1-T^*_2)y=0$ by positive definiteness.

**The dictionary with the Banach transpose.** Write $R_H:H\to H^*$ and $R_K:K\to K^*$ for the Riesz maps $R_H(x)=\langle\,\cdot\,,x\rangle_H$ and $R_K(y)=\langle\,\cdot\,,y\rangle_K$, and let $T'\in\mathcal B(K^*,H^*)$ be the transpose of $T$, $(T'g)(x)=g(Tx)$ ([[def-transpose-of-a-bounded-operator]]). Then for all $y\in K$ and $x\in H$,

$$\bigl(R_H(T^*y)\bigr)(x)=\langle x,T^*y\rangle_H=\langle Tx,y\rangle_K=(R_Ky)(Tx)=\bigl(T'(R_Ky)\bigr)(x),$$

so $R_H\,T^*=T'\,R_K$. The Hilbert adjoint is thus the Banach transpose conjugated by the Riesz identifications of $H$ and $K$ with their duals; it is a different operator from $T'$ whenever the Riesz maps are conjugate-linear.

derivations.claim: [Hilbert-space axioms] [F1] gives sesquilinearity, Hermitian symmetry and positive definiteness of the displayed form, since all of these are checked componentwise and the sum over $l=1,\dots,r$ is finite. For completeness let $(x^{(n)})_{n}$ be a Cauchy sequence in $H$, $x^{(n)}=(x^{(n)}_{l})_{l}$. For each $l$ and all $m,n$ one has $\|x^{(n)}_{l}-x^{(m)}_{l}\|_{l}\le \|x^{(n)}-x^{(m)}\|$, so $(x^{(n)}_{l})_{n}$ is Cauchy in $H_{l}$ and converges to some $x_{l}\in H_{l}$; then $\sum_{l}\|x_{l}\|^{2}= \lim_{n}\sum_{l}\|x^{(n)}_{l}\|^{2} \le\limsup_{n}\|x^{(n)}\|^{2}<\infty$ because a Cauchy sequence is bounded, so $x:=(x_{l})\in H$, and $\|x^{(n)}-x\|^{2}=\lim_{m}\sum_{l}\|x^{(n)}_{l}-x^{(m)}_{l}\|^{2} =\lim_{m}\|x^{(n)}-x^{(m)}\|^{2}$, which tends to $0$ as $n\to\infty$ uniformly in $n$ because the sequence is Cauchy; hence $x^{(n)}\to x$. This proves (a) for the space.

[Density and linearity of the domain] The algebraic sum $\bigoplus_{l}D(A_{l})\subseteq D(A)$: each $(x_{l})$ with $x_{l}\in D(A_{l})$ has a finite sum $\sum_{l}\|A_{l}x_{l}\|^{2}$. It is dense in $H$: given $x\in H$ and $\varepsilon>0$, density of $D(A_{l})$ gives for each $l$ a vector $y_{l}\in D(A_{l})$ with $\|x_{l}-y_{l}\|<\varepsilon/\sqrt r$, so $y:=(y_{l})\in\bigoplus_{l}D(A_{l})$ and $\|x-y\|^{2}=\sum_{l}\|x_{l}-y_{l}\|^{2}<\varepsilon^{2}$. The set $D(A)$ is a linear subspace because $\sum_{l}\|\alpha A_{l}x_{l}+\beta A_{l}y_{l}\|^{2}\le 2|\alpha|^{2}\sum_{l}\|A_{l}x_{l}\|^{2} +2|\beta|^{2}\sum_{l}\|A_{l}y_{l}\|^{2}<\infty$ for $x,y\in D(A)$, and $A$ is linear because each $A_{l}$ is.

[Symmetry] Let $x,y\in D(A)$. Then $\langle Ax,y\rangle=\sum_{l}\langle A_{l}x_{l},y_{l}\rangle_{l} =\sum_{l}\langle x_{l},A_{l}y_{l}\rangle_{l}=\langle x,Ay\rangle$, because each $A_{l}$ is self-adjoint and hence symmetric; all sums are finite.

[The adjoint domain] Let $y\in D(A^{*})$ and $z:=A^{*}y$. For fixed $l$ and each $u\in D(A_{l})$ let $x^{(l,u)}\in H$ have $u$ in slot $l$ and $0$ in all other slots; then $x^{(l,u)}\in D(A)$ and $Ax^{(l,u)}$ has $A_{l}u$ in slot $l$. Using [F2] for $A$ and the componentwise pairing, $\langle A_{l}u,y_{l}\rangle_{l} =\langle Ax^{(l,u)},y\rangle=\langle x^{(l,u)},z\rangle =\langle u,z_{l}\rangle_{l}$ for every $u\in D(A_{l})$. Hence $u\mapsto\langle A_{l}u,y_{l}\rangle_{l}$ is bounded on $D(A_{l})$, represented by $z_{l}$; so $y_{l}\in D(A_{l}^{*})=D(A_{l})$ and $A_{l}^{*}y_{l}=z_{l}$, that is $A_{l}y_{l}=z_{l}$. Summing, $\sum_{l}\|A_{l}y_{l}\|^{2}=\sum_{l}\|z_{l}\|^{2}=\|z\|^{2}<\infty$, so $y\in D(A)$ and $Ay=z$. Hence $D(A^{*})\subseteq D(A)$ and $A^{*}y=Ay$.

[Self-adjointness] Step 1.3 gives symmetry; symmetry gives $D(A)\subseteq D(A^{*})$ with $A^{*}$ agreeing with $A$ there ([[def-adjoint-of-a-densely-defined-unbounded-operator]]), and step 1.4 gives the converse inclusion, so $A^{*}=A$ by [F2]. The norm identity is [F1] applied to $Ax=(A_{l}x_{l})$. This proves (b).

[Bounded sums] Let $B_{l}\in\mathcal B(H_{l})$ and put $M:=\max_{1\le l\le r}\|B_{l}\|$, which exists because the index set is finite and nonempty. For $x\in H$, $\|Bx\|^{2}=\sum_{l}\|B_{l}x_{l}\|^{2} \le M^{2}\sum_{l}\|x_{l}\|^{2}=M^{2}\|x\|^{2}$, so $B$ is bounded with $\|B\|\le M$ by [F3]. If $M>0$, choose $l_{0}$ with $\|B_{l_{0}}\|=M$; since $\|B_{l_{0}}\|>0$, $H_{l_{0}}\ne\{0\}$. For each $\eta>0$, the unit-sphere formula for the operator norm in [F3] gives a unit vector $u_{l_{0}}\in H_{l_{0}}$ with $\|B_{l_{0}}u_{l_{0}}\|>M-\eta$. The vector with $u_{l_{0}}$ in slot $l_{0}$ and $0$ elsewhere is a unit vector of $H$, so $\|B\|\ge\|Bx\|=\|B_{l_{0}}u_{l_{0}}\|>M-\eta$; letting $\eta\downarrow0$ gives $\|B\|\ge M$. If $M=0$, the upper bound already gives $\|B\|=0=M$. Thus $\|B\|=\max_l\|B_l\|$. For $B_{l}^{*}$ the adjoint of $B_{l}$, the operator $\bigoplus_{l}B_{l}^{*}$ satisfies $\langle Bx,y\rangle=\sum_{l}\langle B_{l}x_{l},y_{l}\rangle_{l} =\sum_{l}\langle x_{l},B_{l}^{*}y_{l}\rangle_{l} =\langle x,(\bigoplus_{l}B_{l}^{*})y\rangle$ for all $x,y\in H$, so $B^{*}=\bigoplus_{l}B_{l}^{*}$ by [F3]. If every $B_{l}$ is unitary then $B^{*}B=\bigoplus_{l}B_{l}^{*}B_{l}=\bigoplus_{l}I_{H_{l}}=I$ and likewise $BB^{*}=I$, so $B$ is unitary. This proves (c).

boundaries.reason: The index range $l=1,\dots,r$ with $r\ge1$ is fixed nonempty by the statement, and no empty family, empty sum or empty Borel set is formed; the argument takes no limit over an empty collection.

reviewed.reason: The actual finite component list has r>=1 in the Statement. The detected sums are over l=1,...,r or over a convergence sequence, not a potentially empty component set. Step 1.1 and the norm maximum in (c) use this exact nonempty finite range.

boundaries.evidence: Step 2.1 gives the norm identity at the zero vector, $\|A0\|^{2}=0$, and step 3.1 covers $B_{l}=0$, where $\|B\|=0=\max_{l}\|B_{l}\|$ and $B^{*}=B$; no norm is inverted.

Steps 1.1-1.3 and 3.1 are written for arbitrary $r\ge1$ and at $r=1$ become the scalar statements: every sum has the single term $l=1$, the supremum of step 3.1 is attained at $l_{0}=1$, and $B^{*}=B_{1}^{*}$.

No eigenvalue, multiplicity or spectral-simplicity hypothesis occurs: steps 1.2-1.4 use only dense domains and self-adjointness of $A_{l}$, and a slot with $H_{l}=\{0\}$ contributes the single vector $0$ to the test in step 1.4, leaving $D(A^{*})\subseteq D(A)$ unchanged.
The finite sums of steps 1.1-1.4 and 3.1 run over the full range $l=1,\dots,r$ of the statement, so the endpoint indices $l=1$ and $l=r$ are included; no half-open or truncated range appears.

The statement declares the Axiom of Countable Choice as the choice hypothesis of the cited adjoint definitions, and step 2.1 quotes [F2] under that hypothesis; the proof makes no selection of its own and uses neither dependent nor full choice.

boundaries.reason: The lemma is a list of assertions (a)-(c) about a Hilbert space, self-adjointness, a norm identity and adjoints; no clause is an if-and-only-if, so there is no forward half to check.
No converse is asserted: the lemma does not claim that every self-adjoint operator on $H$ arises as an orthogonal sum of self-adjoint operators on prescribed subspaces.

risk_review.notes: Reviewed all six steps: finite-component completeness, dense product domain, symmetry and slotwise adjoint equality. The bounded-sum norm lower bound is restricted to M>0; if every space/operator is zero the upper bound gives equality. Countable Choice is explicit for adjoint definitions; no arbitrary-index sum is used. Exact adjoint, norm and Hilbert definitions checked on disk. Reader repair accepted.

citations.quote:
Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $H,H',K,K'$ be complex Hilbert spaces and let $S\in\mathcal B(H,H')$, $T\in\mathcal B(K,K')$ be bounded linear operators ([[def-bounded-linear-operator]]). Write $H\widehat\otimes K$ for the completion of the algebraic tensor product constructed in [[lem-nrqm-composites-hilbert-tensor-construction]], with inclusion $\kappa$.

(a) There is a unique bounded linear operator $S\otimes T: H\widehat\otimes K\to H'\widehat\otimes K'$ with $(S\otimes T)\kappa(u\otimes v)=\kappa'(Su\otimes Tv)$ for all $u\in H$, $v\in K$, and it satisfies $\|S\otimes T\|\le\|S\|\,\|T\|$ ([[def-operator-norm]]).

(b) For Hilbert spaces $H'',K''$ and bounded $S':H''\to H$, $T':K''\to K$, one has $(S\otimes T)(S'\otimes T')=(SS')\otimes(TT')$. In particular, for endomorphisms $S:H\to H$, $T:K\to K$, the endomorphisms $S\otimes I_K$ and $I_H\otimes T$ commute and their composite is $S\otimes T$.

(c) The Hilbert adjoint ([[def-hilbert-space-adjoint]]) is $(S\otimes T)^*=S^*\otimes T^*$.

(d) If $S,T$ are unitary, then so is $S\otimes T$. No extension of unbounded maps, and no algebraic manipulation of domains of unbounded operators, is asserted.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space. A finite-valued function $f=u+iv:X\to\mathbb C$ is **measurable** when $u,v$ are real measurable functions. Write
$$N_p(f)=\begin{cases}\left(\int_X|f|^p\,d\mu\right)^{1/p},&\displaystyle\int_X|f|^p\,d\mu<\infty,\\+\infty,&\displaystyle\int_X|f|^p\,d\mu=+\infty,\end{cases}\quad(1\le p<\infty),\qquad N_\infty(f)=\inf\{M\in[0,\infty]:|f|\le M\text{ a.e.}\}.$$
The finite case uses the real power; the infinite case is assigned directly,
so $N_p(f)$ is defined for every measurable finite-valued complex $f$.
The infimum of the empty set of finite bounds is $\infty$; equivalently allow $M=\infty$. Define $\mathcal L^p(\mu;\mathbb C)=\{f:f\text{ measurable},N_p(f)<\infty\}$ and its **set quotient** $L^p(\mu;\mathbb C)=\mathcal L^p/\!\sim$, where $f\sim g$ means $f=g$ a.e. This extends [[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]] and [[def-essential-supremum-with-respect-to-a-measure]]. Norm and vector-space assertions are established separately.

Here $|u+iv|=\sqrt{u^2+v^2}$ and $\overline{u+iv}=u-iv$ as in [[def-complex-conjugate-real-imaginary-part-and-modulus]]. These operations preserve measurability: $u^2+v^2$ is measurable by [[thm-arithmetic-and-lattice-operations-preserve-measurability]], and
$$\{|f|>a\}=\begin{cases}\{u^2+v^2>a^2\},&a\ge0,\\X,&a<0.\end{cases}$$
Thus [[thm-threshold-characterisations-of-real-and-extended-real-measurability]] applies. For $g=a+ib$, the formulas $fg=(ua-vb)+i(ub+va)$ and $\overline f=u-iv$ prove the remaining claims by real arithmetic closure. Nonnegative powers are measurable because $\{r^t>b\}=\{r>b^{1/t}\}$ for $r\ge0,t>0,b\ge0$, with the negative thresholds automatic.

A **finite simple** complex function has finite range and measurable fibers. Its **finite-measure support** condition is $\mu(\{s\ne0\})<\infty$. This concerns the nonzero set, not compactness of its closure. The zero function is an admissible finite simple function, including when $X=\varnothing$ or $\mu(X)=0$.

Integration is componentwise: for integrable $f=u+iv$,
$$\int f\,d\mu=\int u\,d\mu+i\int v\,d\mu.$$
This is the earlier convention of [[def-integrable-real-and-complex-functions-and-their-integrals]] and [[def-l-one-of-a-measure]]. The inequalities $|u|,|v|\le|f|\le|u|+|v|$ show that integrability of the modulus and integrability of both components are equivalent.

For $n\ge1$, define complex $C_c(\mathbb R^n)$, $C_0(\mathbb R^n)$ and $C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^n)$ by requiring both components to lie in the corresponding real spaces ([[def-c-c-and-c-c-infinity-on-rn]], [[def-c-zero-on-rn]]). Derivatives are componentwise, with the multi-index and all-ordered-partials conventions of [[def-ck-and-multi-index-notation-in-several-variables]]. The union of the two compact component supports is compact. A measurable complex $f$ is **locally integrable** for Lebesgue measure if $\int_K|f|<\infty$ on every compact $K$. The component inequalities give the equivalent componentwise condition. By [[thm-heine-borel-rn]], closed bounded balls are compact and each compact set is bounded. Hence compact integrability implies integrability on every bounded open ball by restriction from its closure; conversely each compact set is contained in a bounded open ball. These prove both directions of the ball formulation.

For a topological $X$ with Borel sets contained in $\mathcal A$, define
$$\operatorname{ess\,supp}_\mu f=X\setminus\bigcup\{U:U\text{ open and }f=0\text{ a.e. on }U\}.$$
Changing $f$ on one measurable null set preserves the zero-a.e. property on every $U$, since the union of that set and the old exceptional set is null. Thus essential support depends only on the a.e. class. Ordinary support means $\overline{\{f\ne0\}}$ and can change with the representative.

For the following illustration assume [[def-countable-choice]]. For $f=\mathbf1_{\mathbb Q}$ on $\mathbb R$, [[prop-countable-subsets-of-rn-are-lebesgue-null]] gives $f=0$ Lebesgue-a.e.; therefore $N_\infty(f)=0$ and $\operatorname{ess\,supp}f=\varnothing$, since $U=\mathbb R$ occurs in the union. But [[lem-q-and-irrationals-dense-r]] gives $\overline{\{f\ne0\}}=\mathbb R$. For the Dirac probability measure at zero ([[def-dirac-measure]], [[prop-dirac-measure-is-a-probability-measure]]), the bound $1$ holds everywhere and every $0\le M<1$ fails on $\{0\}$, of measure one. Thus $N_{\infty,\delta_0}(f)=1$.

The raw $L^2$ pairing convention is $\langle f,g\rangle=\int f\overline g$, linear in the first variable. Its integrability and class invariance are obligations of the later pairing items. **Bilinear tests** instead use $\int fs$, with no conjugation of $s$.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space.

- For $0<p<\infty$, define an equivalence relation on $\mathcal L^p(\mu)$ by
  $$f\sim g\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad f-g\in\mathcal N(\mu),$$
  and write $L^p(\mu)$ for the set of classes $[f]$.
- For $p=\infty$, define the same relation on $L^\infty(\mu)$ and again write
  $L^\infty(\mu)$ for the set of classes.

Thus an element of $L^p(\mu)$ is an almost-everywhere equivalence class of
measurable representatives.

When $1\le p\le\infty$, the displayed set quotient agrees with the usual
quotient-vector-space construction of
[[def-quotient-vector-space-and-canonical-projection]].

For $0<p<1$, the same class notation is used; under its stated choice hypothesis, the later item
[[thm-the-l-p-distance-for-zero-less-p-less-one-is-a-complete-translation-invariant-metric]]
supplies the metric structure rather than a normed-space structure.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to [0,\infty]$ be product-measurable. Then
$x \mapsto \int_Y f_x\,d\nu$ and $y \mapsto \int_X f^y\,d\mu$ are measurable,
and

$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

For vectors $u,v$ in a real or complex inner product space,

$$|\langle u,v\rangle|\le\lVert u\rVert\lVert v\rVert.$$

Equality holds if and only if $u$ and $v$ are linearly dependent, including the case in which either vector is zero.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]).

Let $X$ be a normed space, let $D \subseteq X$ be a dense normed subspace, let
$Y$ be a Banach space, and let $T:D\to Y$ be a bounded linear operator. Then
there is a unique bounded linear operator $\widetilde T:X\to Y$ such that

$$\widetilde T|_D = T,$$

and $\|\widetilde T\| = \|T\|$.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let
$(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space and let
$L^2(\mu)$ be the quotient of $\mathcal L^2(\mu)$ by the almost-everywhere zero
functions ([[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]]), with the quotient
norm $\|\cdot\|_2$ ([[thm-the-l-p-norm-descends-to-the-quotient-and-makes-l-p-a-normed-space]]).

1. On **real** $L^2(\mu)$ the formula
   $$\langle f,g\rangle:=\int fg\,d\mu$$is a well-defined inner product, linear in both variables, positive definite, with $\langle f,f\rangle=\|f\|_2^2$; with it $L^2(\mu)$ is a real Hilbert space ([[def-hilbert-space]]). 2. On **complex** $L^2(\mu;\mathbb C)$ the formula$$\langle f,g\rangle:=\int f\overline g\,d\mu$$
   is a well-defined inner product, linear in the first variable and
   conjugate-linear in the second, positive definite, with
   $\langle f,f\rangle=\|f\|_2^2$; with it $L^2(\mu;\mathbb C)$ is a complex
   Hilbert space ([[def-complex-lp-and-euclidean-test-function-conventions]]).

In both cases the inner product induces exactly the established quotient
$L^2$ norm.

derivations.claim: [Well-definedness of $\Psi_{0}$] Let $(f_{l})\in\bigoplus_{l}H$ and let $(\tilde f_{l})$ be another choice of representatives with $\tilde f_{l}=f_{l}$ almost everywhere for each $l$; then $(\tilde f_{1},\dots,\tilde f_{r})=(f_{1},\dots,f_{r})$ almost everywhere, so $\Psi_{0}(f)$ is the same class of $H^{(r)}$ and $\Psi_{0}$ is well defined [F3]. It is complex-linear because addition and scalar multiplication in $H^{(r)}$ are componentwise.

[Isometry] For $f=(f_{l})$ and $g=(g_{l})$ in $\bigoplus_{l}H$, the function $x\mapsto\sum_{l}|f_{l}(x)|^{2}$ is nonnegative and measurable, so [F4] gives $\int_{\mathbb R^{d}}\sum_{l}|f_{l}|^{2} =\sum_{l}\int_{\mathbb R^{d}}|f_{l}|^{2}=\sum_{l}\|f_{l}\|_{H}^{2}$, that is $\|\Psi_{0}(f)\|^{2}=\|f\|^{2}_{\oplus}$; the map $\Psi_{0}$ is thus an isometry. For the inner product, Cauchy-Schwarz gives $\int_{\mathbb R^{d}}\sum_{l}|f_{l}||g_{l}| \le\sum_{l}\|f_{l}\|_{H}\|g_{l}\|_{H} \le\bigl(\sum_{l}\|f_{l}\|^{2}\bigr)^{1/2} \bigl(\sum_{l}\|g_{l}\|^{2}\bigr)^{1/2}<\infty$. Each product $f_l\overline{g_l}$ is integrable by Cauchy-Schwarz, and finite linearity of the Lebesgue integral therefore gives $\langle\Psi_{0}(f),\Psi_{0}(g)\rangle =\int\sum_{l}f_{l}\overline{g_{l}}=\sum_{l}\langle f_{l},g_{l}\rangle_{H}$.

[The tensor identification on the algebraic tensor product] On elementary tensors put $\Theta_{0}(\kappa(u\otimes z)):=\sum_{l}z_{l}\iota_{l}(u)$ for $z=\sum_{l}z_{l}e_{l}$. The map $(u,z)\mapsto\sum_{l}z_{l}\iota_{l}(u)$ $H\times\mathbb C^{r}\to H^{(r)}$ is $\mathbb C$-bilinear, so $\Theta_{0}$ factors through the defining bilinearity relations of the algebraic tensor product $H\odot\mathbb C^{r}$ and is a well-defined complex-linear map ([[lem-nrqm-composites-hilbert-tensor-construction]] clause (a)). Every element of $H\odot\mathbb C^{r}$ can be written as $\sum_{l}w_{l}\otimes e_{l}$: a finite sum $\sum_{i}u_{i}\otimes z_{i}$ equals $\sum_{l}\bigl(\sum_{i}z_{i,l}u_{i}\bigr)\otimes e_{l}$ by bilinearity. For such an element, [F1] gives $\Theta_{0}(\sum_{l}w_{l}\otimes e_{l})=\sum_{l}\iota_{l}(w_{l})=(w_{1},\dots,w_{r})$ and $\|\sum_{l}w_{l}\otimes e_{l}\|^{2}=\sum_{l}\|w_{l}\|^{2} =\|\Theta_{0}(\sum_{l}w_{l}\otimes e_{l})\|^{2}_{H^{(r)}}$. By [F3], every element of $H^{(r)}$ is an $r$-tuple of classes in $H$, so $\Theta_{0}$ is onto $H^{(r)}$. Hence $\Theta_0$ is an isometry of $H\odot\mathbb C^{r}$ onto $H^{(r)}$.
[Surjectivity] Let $g\in H^{(r)}$. By [F3] each component $g_{l}$ is an $L^{2}$ class and $g=(g_{1},\dots,g_{r})=\Psi_{0}((g_{l}))$; hence $\Psi_{0}$ is surjective, and (a) is proved.

[Extension and surjectivity] First $H^{(r)}$ is complete: if $(g^{(n)})_{n}$ is Cauchy, each component sequence $g^{(n)}_{l}$ is Cauchy in the complete scalar space $H$ by [F6] because $\|g^{(n)}_{l}-g^{(m)}_{l}\|_{H}\le\|g^{(n)}-g^{(m)}\|_{H^{(r)}}$. Let $g_l\in H$ be its limit. By [F3] the finite tuple $g=(g_l)$ lies in $H^{(r)}$, and $\|g^{(n)}-g\|_{H^{(r)}}^{2}=\sum_{l=1}^{r}\|g^{(n)}_{l}-g_l\|_{H}^{2}\to0$, so $H^{(r)}$ is complete. By [F5] the isometry $\Theta_{0}$ extends uniquely to a linear isometry $\Theta:H\widehat{\otimes}\mathbb C^{r}\to H^{(r)}$, because $\kappa(H\odot\mathbb C^{r})$ is dense in the completion ([[lem-nrqm-composites-hilbert-tensor-construction]] clause (c)); since $\Theta_0$ is onto by step 1.3, so is $\Theta$. Thus $\Theta$ is unitary. This proves (b) except for the displayed formula, which holds on elementary tensors by construction and extends to all $w$ by continuity of the bounded operators involved.

[Intertwining identities] For $u\in H$ and $z=\sum_{l}z_{l}e_{l}$, $\Theta^{-1}\bigl(a\,\Theta(\kappa(u\otimes z))\bigr) =\Theta^{-1}\bigl(a\sum_{l}z_{l}\iota_{l}(u)\bigr) =\Theta^{-1}\bigl(\sum_{l}z_{l}\iota_{l}(au)\bigr) =\kappa(au\otimes z)=(M_{a}\otimes I)\kappa(u\otimes z)$, where the last identity is [F2]; similarly $\Theta^{-1}\bigl(T_{v}^{(r)}\Theta(\kappa(u\otimes z))\bigr) =\kappa(T_{v}u\otimes z)=(T_{v}\otimes I)\kappa(u\otimes z)$, since $T_{v}^{(r)}$ acts componentwise and $T_{v}^{(r)}\iota_{l}(u)=\iota_{l}(T_{v}u)$ ([[lem-nrqm-magnetic-and-detection-momentum-operators-self-adjoint]] clause (c)). Both sides of each identity are bounded operators (the amplifications are bounded by [F2], and $\Theta$ is unitary by step 2.2), and the elementary tensors have dense span in $H\widehat{\otimes}\mathbb C^{r}$ [F1]; hence the identities hold on all of $H\widehat{\otimes}\mathbb C^{r}$. This proves (c).

Assume the Axiom of Choice and the Axiom of Countable Choice
([[def-axiom-of-choice]], [[def-countable-choice]]). Fix $d\ge1$ and
$\hbar>0$, and let $Q_j,P_j$ be the position and momentum operators of
[[def-nrqm-magnetic-and-detection-position-and-momentum-operators]] on
$L^2(\mathbb R^d;\mathbb C)$; let $\mathcal F_2$ be the unitary Plancherel
transform with $\widehat f(\xi)=\int_{\mathbb R^d}f(x)e^{-2\pi ix\cdot\xi}dx$
on $L^1$ ([[def-fourier-transform-on-l-one-of-rn]], [[thm-plancherel]]).

(a) For every $j$, $Q_j$ is self-adjoint with domain
$D(Q_j)=\{f\in L^2:\ x_jf\in L^2\}$.

(b) For every $j$, $P_j$ is self-adjoint with domain
$$D(P_j)=\{f\in L^2(\mathbb R^d;\mathbb C):\ \xi_j\mathcal F_2f\in L^2(\mathbb R^d;\mathbb C)\},$$
and for every $f\in D(P_j)$, $\mathcal F_2(P_jf)(\xi)=2\pi\hbar\,\xi_j\,\mathcal F_2f(\xi)$
for almost every $\xi$. In particular $P_jf=-i\hbar D_jf$ for every
$f\in W^{1,2}(\mathbb R^d;\mathbb C)$, and for $d=1$ the domain of the single
momentum operator is exactly $D(P)=W^{1,2}(\mathbb R;\mathbb C)$.

(c) For every $a\in\mathbb R^d$ the translation $(T_af)(x):=f(x-a)$ is a
unitary operator, $T_aD(P_j)=D(P_j)$, $T_aP_jT_a^{-1}=P_j$,
$T_aD(Q_j)=D(Q_j)$ and $T_aQ_jT_a^{-1}=Q_j-a_j$ for every $j$; moreover
$D_j(T_af)=T_a(D_jf)$ as $L^2$ classes for every $f\in W^{1,2}$, so $T_a$
preserves $W^{1,2}$ and $W^{2,2}$.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open,
$n\ge1$, let $k\in\mathbb N_0$, and let $u:\Omega\to\mathbb C$ have real
and imaginary parts of class $C^k$. For each multi-index
$\alpha\in\mathbb N_0^n$ with $|\alpha|\le k$, the componentwise classical
derivative $\partial^\alpha u$ is locally integrable and is the weak
derivative $D^\alpha u$. By the uniqueness lemma, it represents the unique
locally integrable weak-derivative class. For $\alpha=0$, this says
$D^0u=u$.

If $\Omega=\varnothing$, the assertion is vacuous: there is only the zero
class and every displayed test identity is zero.

Fix an integer $n\ge1$. With the complex smooth-function convention of [[def-complex-lp-and-euclidean-test-function-conventions]] and multi-indices of [[def-ck-and-multi-index-notation-in-several-variables]], define
$$p_{\alpha\beta}(f)=\sup_{x\in\mathbb R^n}|x^\alpha\partial^\beta f(x)|,\qquad \mathcal S(\mathbb R^n)=\{f\in C^\infty(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb C):p_{\alpha\beta}(f)<\infty\text{ for all }\alpha,\beta\}.$$
The zero multi-index gives $x^0=1$ and $\partial^0f=f$. These are actual smooth functions, not equivalence classes. The notation $C_c^\infty$ uses the support convention in [[def-c-c-and-c-c-infinity-on-rn]].

Pointwise differentiation is linear; thus $p_{\alpha\beta}(f+g)\le p_{\alpha\beta}(f)+p_{\alpha\beta}(g)$ and $p_{\alpha\beta}(cf)=|c|p_{\alpha\beta}(f)$. In particular this set is a complex vector space and each $p_{\alpha\beta}$ is a seminorm. The zero function belongs to it. Since $p_{00}(f)=0$ forces $f(x)=0$ for every $x$, the family separates functions. No choice principle is needed.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Fix integers
$d\ge1$ and $r\ge1$, let $H:=L^{2}(\mathbb R^{d};\mathbb C)$ with the Euclidean
integral pairing ([[def-complex-lp-and-euclidean-test-function-conventions]],
[[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]],
[[lem-l-two-with-the-integral-pairing-is-a-hilbert-space]]), let
$$H^{(r)}:=L^{2}\bigl(\mathbb R^{d};\mathbb C^{r}\bigr),\qquad \langle f,g\rangle:=\int_{\mathbb R^{d}}\sum_{l=1}^{r}f_{l}(x)\overline{g_{l}(x)}\,dx,$$
and let $\mathbb C^{r}$ carry the standard inner product with orthonormal basis
$e_{1},\dots,e_{r}$ ([[def-hilbert-space]],
[[def-orthonormal-family-complete-orthonormal-system-and-hilbert-basis]]).
Write $H\widehat{\otimes}\mathbb C^{r}$ for the completed tensor product of
[[lem-nrqm-composites-hilbert-tensor-construction]] with inclusion $\kappa$.
Then:

(a) the map
$$\Psi_{0}\Bigl((f_{l})\Bigr):=\bigl(x\mapsto(f_{1}(x),\dots,f_{r}(x))\bigr)$$
is a well-defined unitary isomorphism $\bigoplus_{l=1}^{r}H\to H^{(r)}$, and
$$\|\Psi_{0}(f)\|_{H^{(r)}}^{2}=\sum_{l=1}^{r}\|f_{l}\|_{H}^{2},\qquad \langle\Psi_{0}(f),\Psi_{0}(g)\rangle=\sum_{l=1}^{r}\langle f_{l},g_{l}\rangle_{H};$$

(b) the assignment on elementary tensors
$\Theta_{0}(\kappa(u\otimes e_{l})):=\iota_{l}(u)$, where $\iota_{l}(u)$ is
the $r$-tuple with $u$ in slot $l$ and $0$ elsewhere, extends uniquely to a
surjective linear isometry $\Theta:H\widehat{\otimes}\mathbb C^{r}\to H^{(r)}$
(so $\Theta$ is unitary), and
$\Theta(\kappa(u\otimes z))=\sum_{l=1}^{r}z_{l}\,\iota_{l}(u)$ for all
$u\in H$, $z=\sum_{l}z_{l}e_{l}\in\mathbb C^{r}$;

(c) for every $a\in L^{\infty}(\mathbb R^{d})$ and every $v\in\mathbb R^{d}$ one
has the intertwining identities
$$\Theta^{-1}\bigl(a\cdot\Theta(w)\bigr)=(M_{a}\otimes I_{\mathbb C^{r}})w,\qquad \Theta^{-1}\bigl(T_{v}^{(r)}\Theta(w)\bigr)=(T_{v}\otimes I_{\mathbb C^{r}})w\qquad(w\in H\widehat{\otimes}\mathbb C^{r}),$$
where $M_{a}$ is multiplication by $a$, $T_{v}$ is the Euclidean translation
$T_{v}h:=h(\cdot-v)$ of [[lem-nrqm-magnetic-and-detection-momentum-operators-self-adjoint]]
clause (c), $T_{v}^{(r)}$ is its componentwise action on $H^{(r)}$, and the
bounded amplifications are those of [[lem-nrqm-composites-bounded-tensor-maps]].

Fix an integer $n\ge1$. With the complex smooth-function convention of [[def-complex-lp-and-euclidean-test-function-conventions]] and multi-indices of [[def-ck-and-multi-index-notation-in-several-variables]], define
$$p_{\alpha\beta}(f)=\sup_{x\in\mathbb R^n}|x^\alpha\partial^\beta f(x)|,\qquad \mathcal S(\mathbb R^n)=\{f\in C^\infty(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb C):p_{\alpha\beta}(f)<\infty\text{ for all }\alpha,\beta\}.$$
The zero multi-index gives $x^0=1$ and $\partial^0f=f$. These are actual smooth functions, not equivalence classes. The notation $C_c^\infty$ uses the support convention in [[def-c-c-and-c-c-infinity-on-rn]].

Pointwise differentiation is linear; thus $p_{\alpha\beta}(f+g)\le p_{\alpha\beta}(f)+p_{\alpha\beta}(g)$ and $p_{\alpha\beta}(cf)=|c|p_{\alpha\beta}(f)$. In particular this set is a complex vector space and each $p_{\alpha\beta}$ is a seminorm. The zero function belongs to it. Since $p_{00}(f)=0$ forces $f(x)=0$ for every $x$, the family separates functions. No choice principle is needed.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]), the choice
hypothesis of the cited definitions of the adjoint. Fix an integer $r\ge1$, let
$H_{1},\dots,H_{r}$ be complex Hilbert spaces with inner products linear in the
first argument ([[def-hilbert-space]]), and let
$$H:=\bigoplus_{l=1}^{r}H_{l},\qquad \bigl\langle (x_{l}),(y_{l})\bigr\rangle:=\sum_{l=1}^{r}\langle x_{l},y_{l}\rangle_{H_{l}},$$
be their orthogonal sum. For each $l$ let $A_{l}:D(A_{l})\subset H_{l}\to H_{l}$
be a densely defined self-adjoint operator
([[def-adjoint-of-a-densely-defined-unbounded-operator]],
[[def-symmetric-self-adjoint-and-essentially-self-adjoint]]) and put
$$D(A):=\Bigl\{(x_{l})\in H:\ x_{l}\in D(A_{l})\ \text{for all }l,\ \sum_{l=1}^{r}\|A_{l}x_{l}\|_{H_{l}}^{2}<\infty\Bigr\},\qquad A(x_{l}):=(A_{l}x_{l}).$$
Then:

(a) $H$ is a complex Hilbert space, $D(A)$ is a dense linear subspace of $H$,
and $A:D(A)\to H$ is a linear operator;

(b) $A$ is symmetric and self-adjoint, and
$\|Ax\|^{2}=\sum_{l=1}^{r}\|A_{l}x_{l}\|_{H_{l}}^{2}$ for every $x\in D(A)$;

(c) if $B_{l}\in\mathcal B(H_{l})$ for every $l$
([[def-bounded-linear-operator]]), then $B:=\bigoplus_{l=1}^{r}B_{l}$, defined
by $B(x_{l}):=(B_{l}x_{l})$ for all $(x_{l})\in H$, is bounded with
$$\|B\|=\max_{1\le l\le r}\|B_{l}\|$$
([[def-operator-norm]]), its adjoint is
$B^{*}=\bigoplus_{l=1}^{r}B_{l}^{*}$ ([[def-hilbert-space-adjoint]]), and $B$
is unitary if every $B_{l}$ is unitary.

No assertion is made about infinite orthogonal sums: only the finite case is
proved here.

Assume countable choice and let $n\ge1$. Fourier transformation on Schwartz space extends uniquely to a surjective complex-linear isometry $\mathcal F_2:L^2(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb C)\to L^2(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb C)$. It preserves the first-variable-linear inner product, and hence is unitary.

Assume Countable Choice and let $n\ge1$. For every $u\in\mathcal S'(\mathbb R^n)$ and every multi-index $\alpha\in\mathbb N_0^n$,
$$\mathcal F(D^\alpha u)=(2\pi i\xi)^\alpha\mathcal Fu\qquad\text{in }\mathcal S'(\mathbb R^n),$$
where $D^\alpha$ is the distributional derivative of
[[def-ck-and-multi-index-notation-in-several-variables]] and $\mathcal F$ is
the negative-sign $2\pi$-normalized transform. Moreover, if $u=u_f$ and
$D^\alpha u=u_g$ for $L^2$ classes $f,g\in L^2(\mathbb R^n)$ and their regular
distributions, then the unitary Plancherel transforms satisfy
$$\mathcal F_2g(\xi)=(2\pi i\xi)^\alpha\mathcal F_2f(\xi)\qquad\text{for almost every }\xi\in\mathbb R^n.$$
The second assertion compares the Plancherel classes only; it neither asserts
pointwise values of arbitrary representatives nor presupposes any Sobolev-space
notation.

The complex exponential is entire, and

$$ \exp'(z)=\exp z $$

for every $z\in\mathbb C$.

Assume countable choice, let $n\ge1$, and use Lebesgue measure on $\mathbb R^n$. Translation $\tau_hf(x)=f(x-h)$ is an isometry of complex $L^p$ for $1\le p\le\infty$ and depends norm-continuously on $h$ for $p<\infty$.

For complex $K\in L^1$ and $f\in L^p$, the convolution
$$(K*f)(x)=\int K(y)f(x-y)\,dy$$
exists absolutely a.e., defines a measurable class independent of representatives, and satisfies $\|K*f\|_p\le\|K\|_1\|f\|_p$.

If $K_\varepsilon\in L^1(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb C)$ satisfy
$$\int K_\varepsilon=1,\qquad M:=\sup_{\varepsilon>0}\|K_\varepsilon\|_1<\infty,\qquad \int_{|y|\ge\delta}|K_\varepsilon(y)|\,dy\longrightarrow0\quad(\delta>0),$$
then $K_\varepsilon*f\to f$ in $L^p$ for $p<\infty$, and uniformly for $f\in C_0(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb C)$. For fixed $K\in L^1$, $K*f\in C_0$ when $f\in C_0$. These assertions allow complex and sign-changing kernels. In particular $K_\varepsilon(x)=\varepsilon^{-n}K(x/\varepsilon)$ is such an approximate identity whenever $K\in L^1$ and $\int K=1$.

If $\rho\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb R)$ has mass one, $\rho_\varepsilon(x)=\varepsilon^{-n}\rho(x/\varepsilon)$, and $f$ is complex locally integrable, then $\rho_\varepsilon*f$ is smooth and
$$\partial^\alpha(\rho_\varepsilon*f)=(\partial^\alpha\rho_\varepsilon)*f.$$
A compactly supported input gives a compactly supported output. No general $L^\infty$ translation-continuity or approximate-identity convergence is asserted.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $T$ be a self-adjoint operator on $H$ with
spectral projection valued measure $E$, and set
$U(t):=e^{itT}=\int_{\mathbb R}e^{it\lambda}\,dE(\lambda)$ for $t\in\mathbb R$.
Then $U$ is a strongly continuous one-parameter unitary group,
$U(t)D(T)=D(T)$ and $TU(t)=U(t)T$ on $D(T)$, and the derivative
$\lim_{t\to0}\frac1t(U(t)x-x)$ exists exactly for $x\in D(T)$, where it equals
$iTx$. Thus the generator of $U$ is $G=iT$, with $D(G)=D(T)$.

A **strongly continuous one-parameter unitary group** on the complex Hilbert
space $H$ is a map $U:\mathbb R\to\mathcal B(H)$ such that
$U(0)=I$, $U(s+t)=U(s)U(t)$ for all $s,t\in\mathbb R$, each $U(t)$ is unitary
(that is, onto and norm preserving, equivalently $U(t)^*U(t)=U(t)U(t)^*=I$,
[[def-bounded-linear-operator]], [[def-operator-norm]]), and the orbit maps
$t\mapsto U(t)x$ are continuous at every $t$ for every $x\in H$, from the
usual metric on $\mathbb R$ to the norm metric of $H$
([[def-metric-continuity]]).

**Continuity at the origin suffices, and weak continuity is equivalent to
strong continuity.** These two clauses are part of the definition's content
and are proved here. If $t\mapsto U(t)x$ is continuous at $t=0$ and $t_0\in
\mathbb R$, then $U(t)x-U(t_0)x=U(t_0)\bigl(U(t-t_0)x-x\bigr)$ and $U(t_0)$ is
isometric, so $\|U(t)x-U(t_0)x\|=\|U(t-t_0)x-x\|\to0$ as $t\to t_0$; the group
law and isometry turn continuity at one point into continuity everywhere.
Likewise, if $t\mapsto U(t)x$ is merely weakly continuous at $0$, then for
$x\in H$ the expansion $\|U(t)x-x\|^2=2\|x\|^2-2\operatorname{Re}\langle
U(t)x,x\rangle$ shows that norm convergence at $t=0$ follows from
$\langle U(t)x,x\rangle\to\langle x,x\rangle$; and at an arbitrary $t_0$ one has
$U(t)y-U(t_0)y=U(t_0)\bigl(U(t-t_0)y-y\bigr)$, so weak continuity at $t_0$ for
every $y$ follows from the case $t=0$. Conversely, norm continuity of an orbit
implies its weak continuity, since for each fixed $y\in H$, Cauchy--Schwarz
gives
$$|\langle U(t)x-U(t_0)x,y\rangle|\le \|U(t)x-U(t_0)x\|\,\|y\|\longrightarrow0.$$
Finally, a group with
$U(0)=I$ is automatically invertible with $U(t)^{-1}=U(-t)$, so the unitarity
and group clauses are symmetric in $t$.

Let $U$ be a strongly continuous one-parameter unitary group on $H$
([[def-strongly-continuous-one-parameter-unitary-group]]). Its
**infinitesimal generator** is the linear operator $G$ with domain
$$D(G):=\Bigl\{x\in H:\ \lim_{t\to0}\frac1t\bigl(U(t)x-x\bigr)\ \text{exists in }H\Bigr\},\qquad Gx:=\lim_{t\to0}\frac1t\bigl(U(t)x-x\bigr),$$
where this is the two-sided norm limit over real $t\ne0$: it has value $y$
precisely when for every $\varepsilon>0$ there is $\delta>0$ such that
$$0<|t|<\delta\quad\Longrightarrow\quad \left\|\frac{U(t)x-x}{t}-y\right\|<\varepsilon.$$
Equivalently, defining the quotient's value at $t=0$ to be $y$ makes it
continuous there from the usual metric on $\mathbb R$ to the norm metric on
$H$ ([[def-metric-continuity]]). Such a $y$ is unique by the triangle
inequality.

$D(G)$ is a linear subspace and $G$ is linear: if $x,y\in D(G)$ and $a,b$ are
scalars, then $\frac1t(U(t)(ax+by)-(ax+by))=a\frac1t(U(t)x-x)+b\frac1t(U(t)y-y)$
converges with limit $aGx+bGy$, because the operations of $H$ are continuous
and both estimates use the same punctured real parameter $t$; the restriction to $D(G)$
is therefore well defined and linear ([[def-linear-subspace]],
[[def-linear-map]]).

**Sign convention.** This page writes $T=-iG$ for the generator, so that
Stone's theorem reads $U(t)=e^{itT}$ with $T$ self-adjoint; equivalently
$G=iT$. In the convention of Teschl's book one has $U(t)=e^{-itA}$ with $A$
self-adjoint, so $G=-iA$ and hence $A=iG=-T$; every formula below is written in the
$U(t)=e^{itT}$ convention and the translation is recorded where a source is
cited.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. The map $T\mapsto U(t)=e^{itT}$, computed by the
Borel functional calculus of $T$
([[thm-unbounded-borel-functional-calculus]]), is a bijection from the set of
self-adjoint operators on $H$ onto the set of strongly continuous
one-parameter unitary groups on $H$. Its inverse assigns to $U$ its generator
$G$ and the self-adjoint operator $T=-iG$; here $D(T)=D(G)$ is exactly the set
of vectors at which $t\mapsto U(t)x$ is differentiable at $0$, and
$\frac1t(U(t)x-x)\to iTx$ for $x\in D(T)$.

Let $f$ and $(f_n)$ be measurable complex-valued functions such that
$f_n\to f$ almost everywhere and $|f_n|\le g$ almost everywhere for a single
nonnegative measurable function $g$ with $\int g\,d\mu<+\infty$. Then
$f\in L^1(\mu)$,
$$\int|f_n-f|\,d\mu\longrightarrow0,$$
and hence
$$\int f_n\,d\mu\longrightarrow\int f\,d\mu.$$

derivations.claim: [Operators as orthogonal sums] Let $f=(f_{l})\in H^{(r)}$. By [F2] one has $\Psi_{0}^{-1}f=(f_{l})\in\bigoplus_{l}L^{2}$, and $f\in D(Q_{j})$ holds exactly when $x_{j}f_{l}\in L^{2}$ for every $l$, that is when $\Psi_{0}^{-1}f\in\bigoplus_{l}D(Q_{j}^{(1)})$; on that domain $\Psi_{0}^{-1}(Q_{j}f)=(x_{j}f_{l})_{l}=(\bigoplus_{l}Q_{j}^{(1)})\Psi_{0}^{-1}f$. The same computation with $D_{k}f_{l}$ in place of $x_{j}f_{l}$ gives $\Psi_{0}^{-1}(P_{k}f)=(\bigoplus_{l}P_{k}^{(1)})\Psi_{0}^{-1}f$ on $\Psi_{0}^{-1}D(P_{k})=\bigoplus_{l}D(P_{k}^{(1)})$. The finite-sum condition in the domain of an orthogonal sum is automatic here: if every $\|Q_{j}^{(1)}f_{l}\|$ is finite then $\sum_{l}\|Q_{j}^{(1)}f_{l}\|^{2}=\|Q_{j}f\|^{2}<\infty$, and similarly for $P_{k}$. This proves the identification in (a).

[A scalar difference quotient] Let $g\in L^{2}(\mathbb R^{d};\mathbb C)$ with $\xi_{j}\mathcal F_{2}g\in L^{2}$, that is $g\in D(P_{j}^{(1)})$ by [F1], and let $t\ne0$. The modulation identity $\mathcal F_{2}(T_{te_{j}}g)(\xi)=e^{-2\pi it\xi_{j}}\mathcal F_{2}g(\xi)$ of [F4] gives $\mathcal F_{2}\Bigl(\frac1t\bigl(T_{te_{j}}g-g\bigr)\Bigr)(\xi) =\frac{e^{-2\pi it\xi_{j}}-1}{t}\,\mathcal F_{2}g(\xi).$ Writing $\theta:=-2\pi t\xi_{j}$, the factor equals $\frac{e^{i\theta}-1}{i\theta}\cdot\bigl(-2\pi i\xi_{j}\bigr)$; by [F4] the first factor tends to $1$ and $\theta\to0$ for every fixed $\xi$ as $t\to0$, so the pointwise limit of the right-hand side is $-2\pi i\xi_{j}\mathcal F_{2}g(\xi)=\mathcal F_{2}(-D_{j}g)(\xi)$ [F4]. For domination, [F4] gives $|\frac{e^{i\theta}-1}{t}|\le|\theta/t|=2\pi|\xi_{j}|$, so the modulus of the difference $h_t(\xi):=\bigl(\frac{e^{-2\pi it\xi_{j}}-1}{t}+2\pi i\xi_{j}\bigr)\mathcal F_{2}g(\xi)$ is at most $4\pi|\xi_{j}|\,|\mathcal F_{2}g(\xi)|$, whose square is integrable because $\xi_{j}\mathcal F_{2}g\in L^{2}$. Since $h_t\to0$ pointwise, [F6] applied to $|h_t|^{2}$ gives $\int|h_t|^{2}\to0$, so the Fourier-space difference converges to $\mathcal F_{2}(-D_{j}g)$ in $L^{2}$. As $\mathcal F_{2}$ is a surjective isometry [F4], and $-D_{j}g=-\frac{i}{\hbar}P_{j}^{(1)}g$, this yields $\lim_{t\to0}\frac1t\bigl(T_{te_{j}}g-g\bigr)=-\frac{i}{\hbar}P_{j}^{(1)}g \qquad\text{in }L^{2}.$

[Self-adjointness] Each scalar $Q_{j}^{(1)}$ and $P_{k}^{(1)}$ is self-adjoint by [F1], so [F3] makes their finite orthogonal sums self-adjoint with the displayed domains and dense domains; by step 1.1 these sums are the conjugates of $Q_{j}$ and $P_{k}$ by the unitary $\Psi_{0}$, hence $Q_{j}$ and $P_{k}$ are densely defined and self-adjoint. This completes (a).

[Fourier representation] By [F2] and [F3], $\mathcal F_{2}^{(r)}$ is the orthogonal sum of the unitaries $\mathcal F_{2}$, hence unitary. For $f\in D(P_{k})$ its components satisfy $\mathcal F_{2}(P_{k}^{(1)}f_{l})(\xi)=2\pi\hbar\xi_{k}\mathcal F_{2}f_{l}(\xi)$ for almost every $\xi$ by [F1]; assembling components gives $\mathcal F_{2}^{(r)}(P_{k}f)(\xi)=2\pi\hbar\xi_{k}\mathcal F_{2}^{(r)}f(\xi)$ for almost every $\xi$. The domain description follows because $\xi_{k}\mathcal F_{2}f_{l}\in L^{2}$ for all $l$ is exactly $\xi_{k}\mathcal F_{2}^{(r)}f\in L^{2}(\mathbb R^{d};\mathbb C^{r})$. This proves (b).

[Translation identities] By [F2] the translation $T_{a}^{(r)}$ corresponds to $\bigoplus_{l}T_{a}$, which is unitary by [F3] and [F1]; it preserves the componentwise Schwartz and Sobolev classes because each scalar $T_{a}$ does [F1]. The identities $D_{k}(T_{a}^{(r)}f)=T_{a}^{(r)}(D_{k}f)$ and $T_{a}^{(r)}D(Q_{j})=D(Q_{j})$, $T_{a}^{(r)}Q_{j}(T_{a}^{(r)})^{-1}=Q_{j}-a_{j}I$, $T_{a}^{(r)}P_{k}(T_{a}^{(r)})^{-1}=P_{k}$ are componentwise instances of [F1]; for instance, $(T_{a}^{(r)}Q_{j}(T_{a}^{(r)})^{-1}f)_{l} =T_{a}(x_{j}T_{-a}f_{l})=(x_{j}-a_{j})f_{l}$ for $f_{l}\in D(Q_{j}^{(1)})$, and the domain equality follows from the scalar one. This proves (c).

[The componentwise limit] Let $f\in D(P_{j})$. Applying step 1.2 to each component $f_{l}\in D(P_{j}^{(1)})$ and assembling components through the unitary $\Psi_{0}$ [F2] gives $\frac1t(T_{te_{j}}^{(r)}f-f)\to\bigl(-\frac{i}{\hbar}P_{j}^{(1)}f_{l}\bigr)_{l} =-\frac{i}{\hbar}P_{j}f$ in $H^{(r)}$ as $t\to0$; this is the first assertion of (d).

[The group of translations and its generator] Fix $j$. The family $U_{j}(t):=T_{te_{j}}^{(r)}$ is a strongly continuous one-parameter unitary group: the group law and unitarity follow from the componentwise definition of translations and [F3], and strong continuity from [F4]. By step 2.4 its generator $G$ satisfies $G\supseteq-\frac{i}{\hbar}P_{j}$; by [F5] applied to the self-adjoint operator $T:=-P_{j}/\hbar$, the family $V_{j}(t):=\exp\bigl(-\frac{i}{\hbar}tP_{j}\bigr)=\exp(itT)$ is a strongly continuous unitary group with generator $iT=-\frac{i}{\hbar}P_{j}$ and domain $D(P_{j})$, and it preserves $D(P_{j})$ [F5]. On $D(P_{j})$ both groups have the same right derivative at $0$, and both preserve $D(P_{j})$; hence $w(t):=U_{j}(t)g-V_{j}(t)g$ for fixed $g\in D(P_{j})$ satisfies $w'(t)=\bigl(-\frac{i}{\hbar}P_{j}\bigr)w(t)$ and $\frac{d}{dt}\|w(t)\|^{2}=2\operatorname{Re}\langle w(t),-\frac{i}{\hbar}P_{j}w(t)\rangle=0$ because $\langle P_{j}w(t),w(t)\rangle$ is real; with $w(0)=0$ this gives $U_{j}(t)g=V_{j}(t)g$ for all $t$ on the dense set $D(P_{j})$, hence $U_{j}(t)=V_{j}(t)$ by continuity and unitarity. This proves (d).

boundaries.reason: The integers $d,r\ge1$ are fixed, so the coordinate and component index sets are nonempty, and steps 1.1-3.1 form no empty family, empty sum or empty measurable set.

boundaries.evidence: Step 1.1 places the zero class in $D(Q_{j})\cap D(P_{k})$ with $Q_{j}0=P_{k}0=0$, and step 2.2 assigns it the zero multiplication class; the difference quotients of step 1.2 are taken only at $t\ne0$.
Steps 1.2 and 2.4 are proved for the single coordinate direction $e_{j}$ and are therefore exactly the $d=1$ case, while at $r=1$ steps 1.1 and 2.1 assemble one component and every sum has one term.

boundaries.reason: The item identifies maximal domains and spectral measures of the position and momentum components and assumes no eigenvalue, multiplicity or simplicity property; no degenerate spectral case arises.

boundaries.evidence: Step 1.2 forms the difference quotient for every $t\ne0$ and step 2.4 takes the limit $t\to0$, the excluded endpoint of the quotient and the point where the generator identity is asserted; step 2.3 includes the translation parameter $a=0$ with $T_{0}=I$.

The statement assumes the Axiom of Countable Choice and the Axiom of Choice as the choice hypotheses of the cited scalar operator and spectral suppliers, which steps 1.1-3.1 quote; the proof adds no selection of its own.

No converse is asserted: the item does not claim that an arbitrary self-adjoint componentwise operator arises as an orthogonal sum of scalar position or momentum operators.

risk_review.notes: All seven steps checked: scalar maximal domains and Fourier multipliers transport under the finite unitary identification; self-adjointness and density use the orthogonal-sum result. Difference quotient has negative derivative sign, and squared difference is bounded by 16 pi^2 xi_j^2 |F2g|^2, an L1 majorant on D(P_j). The xi_j=0 factor is interpreted by its continuous value (the quotient itself is zero there). Translation/Sobolev invariance and domain equality checked. Step 3.1 compares two flows on their invariant dense domain by constant squared norm, then extends equality, so does not assume an unproved generator-domain equality. AC and Countable Choice explicitly adopted.

citations.quote:
Assume Countable Choice. Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open,
$n\ge1$, let $k\in\mathbb N_0$, and let $u:\Omega\to\mathbb C$ have real
and imaginary parts of class $C^k$. For each multi-index
$\alpha\in\mathbb N_0^n$ with $|\alpha|\le k$, the componentwise classical
derivative $\partial^\alpha u$ is locally integrable and is the weak
derivative $D^\alpha u$. By the uniqueness lemma, it represents the unique
locally integrable weak-derivative class. For $\alpha=0$, this says
$D^0u=u$.

If $\Omega=\varnothing$, the assertion is vacuous: there is only the zero
class and every displayed test identity is zero.

Fix an integer $n\ge1$. With the complex smooth-function convention of [[def-complex-lp-and-euclidean-test-function-conventions]] and multi-indices of [[def-ck-and-multi-index-notation-in-several-variables]], define
$$p_{\alpha\beta}(f)=\sup_{x\in\mathbb R^n}|x^\alpha\partial^\beta f(x)|,\qquad \mathcal S(\mathbb R^n)=\{f\in C^\infty(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb C):p_{\alpha\beta}(f)<\infty\text{ for all }\alpha,\beta\}.$$
The zero multi-index gives $x^0=1$ and $\partial^0f=f$. These are actual smooth functions, not equivalence classes. The notation $C_c^\infty$ uses the support convention in [[def-c-c-and-c-c-infinity-on-rn]].

Pointwise differentiation is linear; thus $p_{\alpha\beta}(f+g)\le p_{\alpha\beta}(f)+p_{\alpha\beta}(g)$ and $p_{\alpha\beta}(cf)=|c|p_{\alpha\beta}(f)$. In particular this set is a complex vector space and each $p_{\alpha\beta}$ is a seminorm. The zero function belongs to it. Since $p_{00}(f)=0$ forces $f(x)=0$ for every $x$, the family separates functions. No choice principle is needed.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice and the Axiom of Choice
([[def-countable-choice]], [[def-axiom-of-choice]]), the choice hypotheses of the
cited scalar operator and spectral suppliers. Fix integers $d\ge1$, $r\ge1$ and
$\hbar>0$. Let $H^{(r)}=L^{2}(\mathbb R^{d};\mathbb C^{r})$ be the
component-valued space of [[lem-nrqm-kinematics-component-valued-wavefunction-identifications]]
with its componentwise inner product, let $Q_{j}^{(1)},P_{k}^{(1)}$ be the
scalar position and momentum operators on $L^{2}(\mathbb R^{d};\mathbb C)$ of
[[def-nrqm-magnetic-and-detection-position-and-momentum-operators]], and let
$\mathcal F_{2}$ be the unitary Plancherel transform with
$\widehat f(\xi)=\int f(x)e^{-2\pi ix\cdot\xi}dx$ on $L^{1}$
([[def-fourier-transform-on-l-one-of-rn]], [[thm-plancherel]]). Write
$\mathcal F_{2}^{(r)}:=\Psi_{0}\bigl(\bigoplus_{l}\mathcal F_{2}\bigr)\Psi_{0}^{-1}$
for its componentwise version, with $\Psi_{0}$ the unitary of
[[lem-nrqm-kinematics-component-valued-wavefunction-identifications]] clause (a).
Define, componentwise,
$$D(Q_{j}):=\bigl\{f=(f_{l})\in H^{(r)}:\ x_{j}f_{l}\in L^{2}\ \text{for all }l\bigr\},\qquad (Q_{j}f)_{l}:=x_{j}f_{l},$$
$$D(P_{k}):=\bigl\{f=(f_{l})\in H^{(r)}:\ D_{k}f_{l}\text{ exists in }L^{2}\ \text{for all }l\bigr\},\qquad (P_{k}f)_{l}:=-i\hbar\,D_{k}f_{l},$$
where $D_{k}$ is the weak derivative of [[def-weak-derivative-of-a-locally-integrable-function]].
Write $W^{m,2}(\mathbb R^{d};\mathbb C^{r})$ for the classes whose components
lie in $W^{m,2}(\mathbb R^{d};\mathbb C)$ ([[def-sobolev-space-wkp-and-its-norm]]),
and $\mathcal S(\mathbb R^{d};\mathbb C^{r})$ for the componentwise Schwartz
class ([[def-schwartz-space-and-its-seminorms]]). Then:

(a) under $\Psi_{0}$ the operators $Q_{j}$ and $P_{k}$ are the orthogonal sums
$\bigoplus_{l}Q_{j}^{(1)}$ and $\bigoplus_{l}P_{k}^{(1)}$ of
[[lem-nrqm-kinematics-orthogonal-sums-of-self-adjoint-operators]]; in particular
$Q_{j}$ and $P_{k}$ are densely defined and self-adjoint with the displayed
domains;

(b) $\mathcal F_{2}^{(r)}$ is unitary,
$$D(P_{k})=\bigl\{f\in H^{(r)}:\ \xi_{k}\mathcal F_{2}^{(r)}f\in L^{2}(\mathbb R^{d};\mathbb C^{r})\bigr\},$$
and for every $f\in D(P_{k})$
$$\mathcal F_{2}^{(r)}(P_{k}f)(\xi)=2\pi\hbar\,\xi_{k}\,\mathcal F_{2}^{(r)}f(\xi)\qquad\text{for almost every }\xi;$$

(c) the componentwise translation $T_{a}^{(r)}f:=f(\cdot-a)$, $a\in\mathbb R^{d}$,
is unitary, leaves $\mathcal S(\mathbb R^{d};\mathbb C^{r})$,
$W^{1,2}(\mathbb R^{d};\mathbb C^{r})$ and $W^{2,2}(\mathbb R^{d};\mathbb C^{r})$
invariant, satisfies $D_{k}(T_{a}^{(r)}f)=T_{a}^{(r)}(D_{k}f)$ for
$f\in W^{1,2}(\mathbb R^{d};\mathbb C^{r})$, and
$$T_{a}^{(r)}D(Q_{j})=D(Q_{j}),\quad T_{a}^{(r)}Q_{j}\bigl(T_{a}^{(r)}\bigr)^{-1}=Q_{j}-a_{j}I,\qquad T_{a}^{(r)}D(P_{k})=D(P_{k}),\quad T_{a}^{(r)}P_{k}\bigl(T_{a}^{(r)}\bigr)^{-1}=P_{k};$$

(d) for every $f\in D(P_{j})$,
$$\lim_{t\to0}\frac1t\bigl(T_{te_{j}}^{(r)}f-f\bigr)=-\frac{i}{\hbar}P_{j}f \qquad\text{in }H^{(r)},$$
so the strongly continuous one-parameter unitary group
$t\mapsto T_{te_{j}}^{(r)}$ has generator $-\frac{i}{\hbar}P_{j}$ and
$$T_{te_{j}}^{(r)}=\exp\Bigl(-\frac{i}{\hbar}tP_{j}\Bigr)\qquad(t\in\mathbb R),$$
the exponential being the spectral-calculus flow of the self-adjoint operator
$P_{j}$.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice and the Axiom of Choice
([[def-countable-choice]], [[def-axiom-of-choice]]), the choice hypotheses of the
cited scalar operator and spectral suppliers. Fix integers $d\ge1$, $r\ge1$ and
$\hbar>0$. Let $H^{(r)}=L^{2}(\mathbb R^{d};\mathbb C^{r})$ be the
component-valued space of [[lem-nrqm-kinematics-component-valued-wavefunction-identifications]]
with its componentwise inner product, let $Q_{j}^{(1)},P_{k}^{(1)}$ be the
scalar position and momentum operators on $L^{2}(\mathbb R^{d};\mathbb C)$ of
[[def-nrqm-magnetic-and-detection-position-and-momentum-operators]], and let
$\mathcal F_{2}$ be the unitary Plancherel transform with
$\widehat f(\xi)=\int f(x)e^{-2\pi ix\cdot\xi}dx$ on $L^{1}$
([[def-fourier-transform-on-l-one-of-rn]], [[thm-plancherel]]). Write
$\mathcal F_{2}^{(r)}:=\Psi_{0}\bigl(\bigoplus_{l}\mathcal F_{2}\bigr)\Psi_{0}^{-1}$
for its componentwise version, with $\Psi_{0}$ the unitary of
[[lem-nrqm-kinematics-component-valued-wavefunction-identifications]] clause (a).
Define, componentwise,
$$D(Q_{j}):=\bigl\{f=(f_{l})\in H^{(r)}:\ x_{j}f_{l}\in L^{2}\ \text{for all }l\bigr\},\qquad (Q_{j}f)_{l}:=x_{j}f_{l},$$
$$D(P_{k}):=\bigl\{f=(f_{l})\in H^{(r)}:\ D_{k}f_{l}\text{ exists in }L^{2}\ \text{for all }l\bigr\},\qquad (P_{k}f)_{l}:=-i\hbar\,D_{k}f_{l},$$
where $D_{k}$ is the weak derivative of [[def-weak-derivative-of-a-locally-integrable-function]].
Write $W^{m,2}(\mathbb R^{d};\mathbb C^{r})$ for the classes whose components
lie in $W^{m,2}(\mathbb R^{d};\mathbb C)$ ([[def-sobolev-space-wkp-and-its-norm]]),
and $\mathcal S(\mathbb R^{d};\mathbb C^{r})$ for the componentwise Schwartz
class ([[def-schwartz-space-and-its-seminorms]]). Then:

(a) under $\Psi_{0}$ the operators $Q_{j}$ and $P_{k}$ are the orthogonal sums
$\bigoplus_{l}Q_{j}^{(1)}$ and $\bigoplus_{l}P_{k}^{(1)}$ of
[[lem-nrqm-kinematics-orthogonal-sums-of-self-adjoint-operators]]; in particular
